subtype: Approach: cramming and rereading instead of practice [Pitfall]
passage: “Samir, come here. You're rereading your notes again. I'm your Bua Parul, and let me tell you about my highlighters. At seventeen, my notes were works of art: four colours, arrows, boxes. I reread them five times and felt wonderful, as if I knew everything. Then came the first mock. The very first question wasn't from my notes, and I couldn't even begin. In three hours I solved eleven problems. My classmate Kusum had fewer pages, but she solved a problem set every single day, and she finished the paper. That afternoon I understood that recognising a page is not the same as producing an answer with a blank sheet in front of you.”

qa.q: How many colours did Parul use in her notes?
How did Parul feel after rereading her notes five times?
qa.a: Wonderful and confident: she felt as if she knew everything, though she had never tested herself.

qa.q: What choice could have changed Parul's mock result, and why?
qa.a: Solving unfamiliar problems from memory before the mock, since practising retrieval would have shown the gaps early.

qa.q: How might Kusum have seen Parul's approach?
qa.a: Kusum, who solved a problem set every day, might have admired the neat notes but noticed that Parul never tested herself on a blank sheet.

grounding: An elder recalls rereading and highlighting notes, feeling prepared, then failing to solve unfamiliar problems in a mock.

subtype: Approach: cramming and rereading instead of practice [Pitfall]
passage:
With only three weeks before the entrance mock and her family's shop needing her every evening during the wedding season, Damini had very little time. So she used it the way that felt most productive: rereading.

Every night after closing the shop she opened her chemistry notes, beautifully written in four colours, and went through them again, highlighting new lines in yellow. By the third week the pages glowed. She felt ready. "I've read organic chemistry six times," she told her friend Noor.

"Have you solved any problems?"

"I don't need to. I know it."

At the mock, the first organic question was one she'd never seen in that form. She stared. The reaction was in her notes, she could picture the page, the colour of the ink. But she couldn't pull the answer out of her head.

She scored 38. Noor, who had done fewer pages and more problems, scored 61.

qa.q: How many times had Damini read organic chemistry?
How did Damini feel before the mock, and during it?
qa.a: Before, she felt confident and ready; during the mock she felt stuck and panicked, unable to recall what she could picture on the page.

qa.q: What would have used her limited time better?
qa.a: Spending part of each evening solving practice problems and testing herself, so she learns to pull answers out rather than just recognise notes.

qa.q: How might Noor see Damini's result?
qa.a: Noor probably feels sympathetic and a bit worried, since Noor's own practice-heavy approach worked better.

grounding: Shows a student, short of time, rereading and highlighting notes and feeling prepared, then failing unfamiliar problems in the mock because she never practised recall.

subtype: Approach: cramming and rereading instead of practice [Pitfall]
passage:
In their Pune flat, Kavitha's chemistry notes were the prettiest in the class. Colour-coded, tabbed, highlighted twice. Her mother liked to show them to guests.

For the whole month before the first mock, Kavitha reread them every evening. Each time, they felt more familiar. "I know this so well now," she told her friend Farida over the phone.

"Try the question bank?" Farida suggested. "Mr. Joshi said to."

"Later. I want to finish revising first."

She never got to it.

At the mock, question five asked about a reaction she'd read ten times, but with a new compound. She could see the page in her mind, even the pink highlighter. She couldn't work out the answer.

Afterwards she sat on the steps outside the exam hall. Farida came out smiling, then saw her face. "The rereading didn't help, did it?" Kavitha shook her head.

qa.q: Who suggested trying the question bank?
qa.a: Farida suggested it, saying Mr. Joshi had told them to.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel sitting on the steps after the mock?
qa.a: She felt shocked and disappointed, realising the familiar-feeling notes had not prepared her.

qa.q: What would you change first in Kavitha's revision?
qa.a: Replace some rereading with the question bank and self-testing, so she practises using the ideas on new problems.

qa.q: How might Farida have felt seeing Kavitha's face?
qa.a: Farida probably felt sorry and concerned, and perhaps uneasy about that earlier smile.

grounding: Shows a student rereading and highlighting notes until they feel familiar, then being unable to solve new problems in the mock because she never practised recall.
